name: Antares 230+ (retired 2023)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Antares (rocket)
sources.note: 200-series first stage empty 20,600 kg, gross 262,600 kg, thrust 3,844 kN, Isp 311.9 / 339.2 s, burn 215 s; Castor 30XL gross 26,300 kg, propellant 24,200 kg, thrust 474 kN, burn 156 s; payload to LEO 8,000 kg; diameter 3.9 m; launch site MARS LP-0A; 230+ last flew 2 August 2023

notes: Single source, so nothing here is cross-checked. Derived, not published: first-stage propellant = gross - empty (242,000 kg); second-stage dry = gross - propellant (2,100 kg); second-stage Isp = thrust x burn time/ (propellant x g0) = 311.6 s, which treats the quoted MAXIMUM thrust as constant and is therefore an upperestimate for a solid motor. The source gives one first-stage thrust figure (3,844 kN) without saying sea-level or vacuum, so it is used as is rather than averaged. The 8,000 kg figure has no stated orbit. The vehicle is retired; it is in the library as a real cargo-to-ISS launcher with a different pad and latitude from the other two. Modelling conventions (assumptions, not data): first-stage thrust and Isp are the mean of the published sea-level and vacuum values because the simulator has one of each per stage; cd = 0.3 is assumed; area is the circle of the published core diameter; fairing mass and jettison are not modelled.

sim_validation.note: Heaviest payload reaching perigee >= 160 km, due east from mars_lp0a (resolved to +/- 250 kg; pitch program [4.263, 9.523, -7.63, 0.78, 0.549] found by CMA-ES seed 7). Orbit reached: 162 x 187 km, max q 41.7 kPa. Published figure: 8000 kg.

name: Atlas V 401

sources.title: ULA: Atlas V
sources.note: 401 performance: 9,800 kg to LEO (200 km circular, 28.7 deg), 8,910 kg to ISS orbit (407 km, 51.6 deg);RD-180 sea-level Isp 311 s; RL10 Isp 450.5 s

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atlas V
sources.note: CCB empty 21,054 kg, propellant 284,089 kg, thrust 3,827 kN SL / 4,152 kN vac, Isp 311.3 / 337.8 s; Centaur III empty 2,316 kg, propellant 20,830 kg, thrust 99.2 kN, Isp 450.5 s, diameter 3.81 m

notes: Not crew rated in this configuration: the crewed Atlas V is the N22 (two solid boosters, dual-engine Centaur), which the two-serial-stage simulator cannot represent, so it is not in the library. The Centaur'sarea uses the core diameter (3.81 m), not its own 3.05 m, because it flies inside the fairing. The 4 m fairing mass is not in either source. The published 9,800 kg is to 200 km circular at 28.7 deg (ULA), whichis the same reference orbit the validation uses. Source status: 'Active, retiring'. KNOWN MODEL LIMITATION, measured not assumed: the ascent simulator reaches only 4,410 kg here, 55 % below the published 9,800 kg, and that is the simulator's fault rather than the data's. Centaur has a thrust-to-weight of 0.31 at staging and would burn for 928 s continuously in this model, because the model has no coast and no second burn. The real flight coasts and relights; burning a 0.31 g stage straight through instead pours the margin into gravity losses. The other two vehicles, whose upper stages sit at 0.84 and 1.41, come out within tolerance. Expect this to improve when WP2-02's MissionEnv replaces the single continuous burn with discrete burns and coasts. Modelling conventions (assumptions, not data): first-stage thrust and Isp are the mean of the published sea-level and vacuum values because the simulator has one of each per stage; cd = 0.3 is assumed; area is the circle of the published core diameter; fairing mass and jettison are not modelled.

sim_validation.note: Heaviest payload reaching perigee >= 160 km, due east from ccsfs_slc41 (resolved to +/- 153 kg; pitch program [12.017, 17.457, 13.247, 0.414, 1.15] found by CMA-ES seed 7). Orbit reached: 175 x 225 km, max q 99.8 kPa. Published figure: 9800 kg.

notes: Crew-capable class: SpaceX describes Falcon 9 as transporting people, and it launches Crew Dragon. Conflicts between sources: second-stage thrust is 981 kN on spacex.com and in the stage table but 934 kN inthe Wikipedia infobox (981 kN used, manufacturer value). The stage masses sum to 517,870 kg against a published lift-off mass of 549,054 kg; the difference (about 31 t) is consistent with payload plus fairingbut is not itemised by any source. The published 22,800 kg is the expendable figure to a 28.5 deg orbit; no altitude is stated. No source publishes a max-q limit. Modelling conventions (assumptions, not data): first-stage thrust and Isp are the mean of the published sea-level and vacuum values because the simulator has one of each per stage; cd = 0.3 is assumed; area is the circle of the published core diameter; fairing mass and jettison are not modelled.
